title: Sliding-window rate limits and token overage billing
scenario: Replay a day of per-tenant API requests through a sliding-window limiter (plan limits, overrides, 0 = suspended), tally allowed/billable usage, and invoice overage tokens with half-up cent rounding.

verified.why_correct: It looks like it should exclude 4xx responses as well, but README rule 5 bills client errors and only drops 5xx, so `status < 500` is exactly the rule. tally() only calls it for allowed requests.

bugs.title: Window left in milliseconds
bugs.symptom: Test 1 test_throttled_requests: acme [a04, a05, a06], cove [c03, c04], fern [f04, f05, f06], gale [g05, g06]. Test 2: acme allowed 3, billable tokens acme 1200 / fern 1800 / gale 8000. Test 3: acme 0.08, fern 0.32, gale 0.75; total 5.61.
bugs.why: Plan.window is compared with ages in seconds, but window_ms is milliseconds. Without the /1000 the window is 60,000 s (almost 17 hours), so every allowed request of the day stays in the window.
bugs.unblocks: Most of the throttling in Test 1, plus the allowed counts and tokens for acme, cove, fern and gale. Exposes B2.
hints: acme's 10:03 request is throttled though the previous ones are minutes old. How long does the window seem to be?
Check the units of Plan.window against what age_seconds returns.
probes: Why was bolt's next-day traffic unaffected by this?
Where else would you look for unit mismatches in this codebase?

bugs.title: Request exactly one window old counted as inside
bugs.symptom: Only visible after B1 is fixed. Test 1: acme throttled [a04] instead of [a05]. Test 2: acme billable tokens 1900. Test 3: acme overage 900, amount 0.36, total 8.31.
bugs.why: The window is (t - window, t], so a request exactly 60 s old has dropped out. `<=` keeps it, so acme's a04 (exactly 60 s after a01) sees 3 recent requests and is throttled, which then frees a slot for a05.
hints: acme now throttles a04 instead of a05. How far apart are a01 and a04?
Read rule 3 about the window boundary, then the filter in allow().
probes: Why was this invisible while the window was in milliseconds?
fern's f06 is also exactly 60 s after f02, yet it wasn't affected. Why?

bugs.title: Override of 0 falls back to the plan limit
bugs.old: return plan.limit if override is None else override
bugs.symptom: Test 1 test_effective_limits: t-echo 5 instead of 0, and echo throttles nothing. Test 2: echo allowed 2, tokens 7000, by_endpoint {/v1/chat: 2}. Test 3: echo overage 2000, amount 0.50, total 8.77.
bugs.why: `override or plan.limit` treats a parsed 0 like a missing override, so the suspended tenant gets the growth plan's 5 requests per window.
bugs.unblocks: echo's rows in all three tests.
hints: t-echo has a limit_override. What does README rule 1 say it means?
Look at how effective_limit chooses between the override and the plan.
Return `plan.limit if override is None else override`.
probes: Why did t-cove's override of 2 work even with this code?
What would a blank override have produced if the code used `int(text or 0)`?

bugs.title: timedelta.seconds drops the days
bugs.symptom: Test 1: bolt throttled [b06, b07] (its next-day requests). Test 2: bolt (5, 2), tokens 10000, chat 4 / embed 1. Test 3: bolt overage 5000, amount 1.25, total 7.09.
bugs.why: `.seconds` is only the seconds component (0-86399) and ignores `.days`. bolt's requests a day apart look 10-50 s old, so the next-day burst is throttled as if it continued the previous day's window.
bugs.unblocks: bolt's rows in all three tests.
hints: bolt's b06 and b07 are a full day after its other traffic. Why would they be throttled?
Look at how the age of a previous request is computed.
probes: What would `.seconds` return for a negative timedelta of -10 seconds?
Why did all of the other tenants come out right?

bugs.title: Endpoint counter shared by every tenant
bugs.old:
billable_tokens = 0

    def __init__(self, tenant_id):
        self.tenant_id = tenant_id
        self.by_endpoint = Counter()
bugs.new:
billable_tokens = 0
    by_endpoint = Counter()

    def __init__(self, tenant_id):
        self.tenant_id = tenant_id
bugs.symptom: Test 2 test_by_endpoint only: every tenant shows the same inflated counts (chat 40, embed 24 in a full run). The counter is shared across tenants and across build_report() calls, so the numbers depend on how many times the report was built.
bugs.why: A Counter defined on the class is one object shared by all instances, and `row.by_endpoint[...] += 1` mutates it in place. The int counters are fine because `+=` on an int rebinds an instance attribute.
hints: Every tenant shows the same endpoint counts. Where does each tenant's counter come from?
Look at the attributes of TenantUsage.
Create the Counter in __init__: self.by_endpoint = Counter().
probes: Why do allowed/throttled/billable_tokens behave correctly as class attributes?
Would by_endpoint = {} at class level behave differently?

bugs.title: Banker's rounding on invoice amounts
bugs.symptom: Test 3 only: test_invoice_amounts shows bolt 2.42 and gale 2.92 (should be 2.43 / 2.93); total 8.25 instead of 8.27.
bugs.why: round() on a Decimal uses the context's ROUND_HALF_EVEN, so 2.425 → 2.42 and 2.925 → 2.92. The README rounds halves up.
hints: bolt and gale are each one cent short. What are their unrounded amounts?
Look at how charge() rounds to the cent.
probes: Why were acme, cove and dune unaffected?
Would float arithmetic have given 2.93 for gale? Why or why not?

context_qa.q: What order does build_report() run things in?
context_qa.a: It loads plans, then tenants (resolving each tenant's limit with effective_limit), then requests for known tenants. `limiter.run` returns an allowed/throttled decision per request id, `usage.tally` builds a TenantUsage per tenant, and `billing.invoice` turns each usage into an invoice. `billing.total` sums the amounts.

context_qa.q: What units is Plan.window in, and where is it set?
context_qa.a: The dataclass comment says seconds. It is set in `plans.load_plans` from the plan's `window_ms` value in plans.json.

It takes the tenant's stored list of previously allowed timestamps, keeps those whose `age_seconds(ts, prev)` passes the window comparison, and throttles if the kept list has at least `tenant.limit` entries. Otherwise it appends `ts` and stores the kept list as the new history.

context_qa.q: In what order does run() feed requests to the limiter?
context_qa.a: `sorted(requests, key=lambda r: r.ts)`. Python's sort is stable, so equal timestamps keep the order they were loaded in.
Class-level defaults for `allowed`, `throttled` and `billable_tokens`, plus the attributes set in `__init__`. `tally` increments the counters and the per-endpoint counts for each request.

context_qa.q: How is an invoice amount computed?
context_qa.a: `overage` subtracts the plan's included tokens (floored at 0) and `charge` multiplies by `price_per_1k` as a Decimal, divides by 1000 and rounds to cents. The report converts the Decimal to a string.

context_qa.q: Where does price_per_1k come from when plans.json has it as a JSON number?
context_qa.a: `load_plans` does `Decimal(str(spec["price_per_1k"]))`, so 0.15 becomes Decimal('0.15') rather than the binary float's expansion.
